tagline: Hamlet roads in a township that would not be Hammondsburgh.
intro: Winding township roads tie together the old hamlets of Bath, from Ghent, where Yellow Creek was turning mills as early as 1815, up through Bath Center toward Ira and the edge of the Cuyahoga Valley. Houses, mills and cemeteries of the nineteenth century line the way.

For a time the township was called Hammondsburgh, after Jason Hammond, who settled in 1810. Jonathan Hale, another early resident, asked that it be called "Jerusalem, Jericho, Bath, or anything but Hammondsburgh," and in 1818 it became Bath.

moments.title: Ghent Woolen Mill
moments.text: Built in 1832 and called the oldest woolen mill left in Ohio, it never did much trade, since wolves made sheep hard to keep and fleece ran short.

moments.title: Bath Center Cemetery
moments.text: Among burials going back to 1804 stands a stone vault of 1913, built to hold the winter's dead while the ground was too frozen to dig.

moments.title: Hale Farm and Village
moments.text: Jonathan Hale's homestead, its house built in 1825, is now Hale Farm and Village, spread on both sides of Oak Hill Road inside Cuyahoga Valley National Park.
